Does X-Boost or Power Lifting really let a small power station run a 1,500 W load?

Power basics Updated 2026-08-08

X-Boost and Power Lifting are the same idea under two brand names: the machine lowers its output voltage so a heating element draws fewer watts, and a load above the inverter’s continuous rating keeps working at reduced power. It is a real feature and it does something real.

Every verdict on this site is computed as though it were not there. One machine here publishes 600 W continuous and a boost figure of 1,500 W; against a kettle drawing exactly 1,500 W our engine still returns a no, decided on continuous output. That is a deliberate choice, and it costs something.

Show the working →

The third row is the control. It shows what a verdict looks like when the continuous rating is doing the work, and it is the same shade of answer a reader would get anywhere on this site. Our marginal threshold is 82% of continuous output, so a load can be inside the rating and still not be called a clean pass. Boost changes none of that arithmetic, because it never enters it.

Why we leave it out

What the records actually say about boost

The published figures, and one row that prints no figure on purpose. Note what is missing from all of them: a manufacturer statement of which load types the feature is valid for.

BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 — boost output 1,500 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence See the record →
EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus — boost output 1,200 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-09 · high confidence See the record →
BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 — boost output 2,700 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · high confidence See the record →
EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus — boost output Manufacturer sources disagree — under review escalated for manual adjudication See the record →

Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · station records · boost mode

The fourth row is the one to read carefully. That machine’s boost figure is not withheld and not missing — it is in CONFLICT: two official EcoFlow surfaces give two different numbers for the same US model. We have escalated it and not adjudicated it, so the row shows the conflict rather than picking a side. A specification a manufacturer states twice, differently, is exactly the kind of number a verdict should not rest on.

The three reasons, stated as ours rather than as facts about the hardware

First, scope. The mechanism these records describe works by lowering output voltage, which suits a heating element and has no defined behaviour on a motor or a compressor — and the applies_to_load_types field on the BLUETTI records here reads unknown, meaning we have found no maker statement of the boundary. Second, duration. A continuous output rating is a promise about running indefinitely; we have found no published statement of how long a boosted output may be held. Third, and most simply: a verdict has to mean one thing. If some rows counted a boost figure and others did not, the ranked lists on this site would be comparing two different quantities in one column.

The cost of that choice is real and worth naming. On 7 of 12 machines here, our verdicts are stricter than the box. Someone who buys on our answer and then finds their kettle boils anyway is not the victim of an error; they have found the margin we chose to keep. The reverse mistake — calling a 600 W inverter a 1,500 W inverter, and being wrong on the one load where the mechanism does not apply — is the one we are not willing to make.

A boost figure is not a surge rating

This is the confusion with the sharpest consequences, and one record in this library states it outright. BLUETTI gives no surge peak for the Elite 200 V2 — only a Power Lifting figure — and that record’s own note says the two are different quantities and must not be substituted for one another. Our engine honours that: with no published surge figure it falls back to the continuous rating as the start-up ceiling, which is the conservative reading and is why that machine refuses motor loads a bigger surge number might have carried. Boost is about holding a large steady load at reduced voltage. Surge is about surviving the fraction of a second when a motor’s rotor is stalled. Nothing about the first predicts the second.

Questions people ask

What is X-Boost on an EcoFlow power station?
It is a mode that lowers the output voltage so a high-power resistive load — a kettle, a heater, a hair dryer — draws fewer watts and keeps working above the inverter’s continuous rating. BLUETTI sells the same idea as Power Lifting. The records here carry the published figure for each machine that has one.
Why do your verdicts ignore X-Boost and Power Lifting?
Three reasons, and all three are our choice rather than a claim about the hardware. The scope field that would name which load types a boost figure is valid for reads unknown on these records. We have found no published statement of how long a boosted output may be held, where a continuous rating is a promise about running indefinitely. And a verdict column has to mean one thing throughout, which it would not if some rows counted the feature and others did not.
Can a 600 W power station run a 1,500 W kettle?
One machine here publishes exactly that pair of numbers — 600 W continuous, a 1,500 W boost figure — and our engine returns a refusal on continuous output against a kettle drawing 1,500 W. The maker’s feature may well boil your water. Our answer is about what the inverter is rated to hold, and we would rather be strict than be wrong on the load where the mechanism does not apply.
